questions.stem: Choose the correct passive form of: 'The cat ate the mouse.'

options.option_text: The mouse is eaten by the cat.
The mouse was eaten by the cat.
The mouse has been eaten by the cat.
The mouse ate the cat.

questions.explanation: B is correct. 'The cat ate the mouse' is simple past active. Passive rule: Object + was/were + V3 + by + Subject. 'Mouse' (object) + 'was' (past) + 'eaten' (V3) + 'by the cat' (subject). Option A uses 'is' (present), C uses 'has been' (present perfect) — both wrong tense.

questions.stem: Choose the correct passive form of: 'She is writing a novel.'

options.option_text: A novel is written by her.
A novel was being written by her.
A novel is being written by her.
A novel will be written by her.

questions.explanation: C is correct. Present continuous active → passive uses: is/are + being + V3. 'She is writing' → 'A novel is being written by her.' Option A ('is written') is simple present passive. Option B ('was being') is past continuous passive — wrong tense.

questions.stem: Choose the correct passive form of: 'He will announce the results tomorrow.'

options.option_text: The results will be announced by him tomorrow.
The results are announced by him tomorrow.
The results were announced by him tomorrow.
The results would be announced by him tomorrow.

questions.explanation: A is correct. Future simple active → passive: will + be + V3. 'He will announce' → 'The results will be announced by him.' 'Tomorrow' stays. Option D ('would be') is conditional, not future — wrong.

questions.stem: Choose the correct passive form of: 'They have completed the project successfully.'

options.option_text: The project has been completed successfully by them.
The project had been completed successfully by them.
The project was completed successfully by them.
The project is being completed successfully by them.

questions.explanation: A is correct. Present perfect active → passive: has/have + been + V3. 'They have completed' → 'The project has been completed.' Option B uses 'had been' (past perfect) — wrong tense. Option C uses simple past — wrong. Adverb 'successfully' stays in the passive.

questions.stem: Choose the correct passive form of: 'You must submit this form before noon.'

options.option_text: This form is submitted before noon.
This form must be submitted before noon.
This form has to submitted before noon.
This form should have been submitted before noon.

questions.explanation: B is correct. Modal active → passive: modal + be + V3. 'Must submit' → 'must be submitted.' The agent (you) is dropped as it is implied. Option C is grammatically incorrect ('has to submitted' is missing 'be'). Option D changes the modality entirely.

questions.stem: Choose the correct passive form of the interrogative: 'Who is writing this report?'

options.option_text: Who is this report being written by?
By whom is this report being written?
By whom this report is being written?
By whom was this report written?

questions.explanation: B is correct. Interrogative passive: 'Who' (subject-question) → 'By whom' (object-question) + auxiliary inversion. Present continuous: 'is being written'. Correct form: 'By whom is this report being written?' Option A is informal and places 'by' at the end — acceptable in speech but not in formal exam English. Option C lacks auxiliary inversion (no '?'-inversion). Option D uses past tense.

questions.stem: Choose the correct passive form of: 'The police arrested the suspect last night.'

options.option_text: The suspect was arrested by the police last night.
The suspect has been arrested by the police last night.
The suspect is arrested by the police last night.
The suspect was being arrested by the police last night.

questions.explanation: A is correct. Simple past active → 'was/were + V3'. 'Arrested' → 'was arrested'. Time expression 'last night' confirms past tense. Option B ('has been') is present perfect — incompatible with 'last night'. Option D ('was being') is past continuous passive — implies the arrest was interrupted.

questions.stem: Choose the correct passive form of: 'People consider him an expert.'

options.option_text: He is considered an expert by people.
He was considered an expert by people.
He has been considered an expert by people.
An expert is considered him by people.

questions.explanation: A is correct. 'People consider him an expert' → passive: 'He is considered an expert (by people).' Note: In 'consider + object + complement' constructions, the object complement ('an expert') remains after the verb in the passive. Option D wrongly makes 'expert' the subject. Option B/C use wrong tenses.

questions.stem: The active sentence 'The thief broke into the house' has the following passive voice form:

options.option_text: The house was broken in by the thief.
Into the house was broken by the thief.
The house was broken into by the thief.
The house has been broken into by the thief.

questions.explanation: C is correct. 'Break into' is a phrasal verb and must be kept together in the passive. The preposition 'into' cannot be separated from 'break'. So: 'The house was broken into by the thief.' Option A ('broken in') drops 'to' — changes meaning. Option B unnaturally fronts 'into'. Option D uses present perfect — wrong tense for a past event.

questions.stem: The sentence 'It is said that he knows the secret.' can be rewritten in passive form as:

options.option_text: He is said to know the secret.
He said to know the secret.
He is said knowing the secret.
He is said that he knows the secret.

questions.explanation: A is correct. Reporting verb passive conversion: 'It is said that + S + V' → 'S + is said + to + V (infinitive)'. 'he knows' → 'he is said to know'. Option B lacks the auxiliary 'is'. Option C uses a gerund ('knowing') incorrectly. Option D is a common error — it repeats 'that he' after the passive, which is redundant and wrong.
